newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Georgia says ending envoy's immunity moral gesture.
newsitem.headline: Georgia says ending envoy's immunity moral gesture.

text.p: Georgian leader Eduard Shevardnadze said on Sunday that moral principle had persuaded him to waive the diplomatic immunity of one of his diplomats alleged to have caused a fatal U.S. car crash.

"Frankly, it was with grave feelings and a heavy heart that I made the decision regarding the fate of the young and doubtlessly talented diplomat, Georgy Makharadze," he said. But "I cannot imagine diplomacy and politics devoid of moral principle."

"My decision ... must not be considered as though a large country has brought a small one to its knees," Shevardnadze said in a statement recorded on Saturday evening and released in translation on Sunday.
U.S. officials have hailed as courageous Friday's announcement by Shevardnadze that he was prepared to lift Makharadze's diplomatic immunity so he can face charges.

The U.S. attorney's office said last week it believed it had sufficient evidence to prosecute Makharadze, 35, over last Friday's five-car smash that killed a 16-year-old Brazilian girl living in Kensington, Maryland.
The Georgian president also called for new rules governing the granting of immunity to diplomats facing criminal charges.
"New relations call for a new set of guidelines governing the operation of diplomatic services," said Shevardnadze, a former Soviet foreign minister who played a major role in ending the Cold War.
"Often, the mantle of the state succeeds in protecting the diplomat while the average citizen ... suffers," he said.

The United States has not yet brought formal charges against Makharadze. But if diplomatic immunity is waived, prosecutors in the attorney's office plan to move fast and present evidence to a grand jury for a possible indictment, federal law enforcement officials said.
Makharadze sought to leave the United States on Thursday but was returned to Washington, U.S. officials said on Friday.

They said the diplomat set off by car for New York to catch an outbound flight but returned to Washington after U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher voiced concern that his departure would violate a Georgian government pledge.

On Friday U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns praised Shevardnadze's decision. "It's a courageous step. It's highly unusual in modern diplomacy to see a head of state take such a responsible and courageous position," he said.
U.S. law enforcement officials said action could occur within a week and possible charges included negligent homicide, second-degree murder or involuntary manslaughter, depending on the evidence.

Although Shevardnadze's statement did not itself waive immunity, White House press secretary Mike McCurry said the United States saw it as a commitment to do so if charges are filed. "The statement is clear to that effect," he said.
Shevardaze also called for greater openness on spies based in diplomatic missions abroad.

"It is common knowledge that under the roofs of diplomatic missions various state agencies are sheltered," he said. "Why not place on the agenda an increased transparency regarding the activities of all agencies including those that gather intelligence?"
